name: Mars One
operator: Mars One Foundation (Netherlands) and Mars One Ventures AG (Switzerland)
short_status: Cancelled: a one-way Mars settlement announced in 2012 for a 2023 landing, funded by broadcast rights. Nothing was built, and a Basel court declared the for-profit arm, Mars One Ventures AG, bankrupt on 15 January 2019.
tagline: Mars One Foundation (Netherlands) and Mars One Ventures AG (Switzerland) · Europe · Programme · 2012 · The long occupation Cancelled
stats: completed applications, against the 200,000 figure Mars One publicised
Lansdorp's own estimate for landing the first four settlers; it was never raised
pieces of flight hardware built and launch contracts signed

facts.label: What it proposed
facts.value: A permanent human settlement on Mars, established by crews of four arriving every two years, with no return vehicle in the plan at all. That was not an oversight. Mars One argued that leaving out the return halves the problem, and it is true that it does. It also means that everything which follows has to work forever, which is the part that was never costed.

facts.label: Who ran it
facts.value: Bas Lansdorp, a Dutch mechanical engineer who had previously founded a wind-energy company, as chief executive, and Arno Wielders as chief technical officer and co-founder. English Wikipedia dates the founding to 2012, and international coverage describing the plan was running by early June that year.

facts.label: The funding idea
facts.value: Broadcast rights. Mars One's public argument was that the selection, training and journey of the first settlers would be the largest media event in history and that the rights would fund the mission. Speaking at a public debate in August 2015, Lansdorp is reported to have claimed Mars One could make eight times what the Olympics makes from television.

facts.label: The published roadmap
facts.value: As it stood after the December 2013 announcement of a robotic precursor: a demonstration lander and a communications satellite in 2020, rovers in 2022, six cargo missions in 2024, the first crewed landing in 2025 and a second crew in 2026. Earlier statements had put the first landing in 2023. No element of this schedule was ever met, and no element of it was ever begun as hardware.

facts.label: The roadmap, revised twice
facts.value: On 19 March 2015 Lansdorp announced the first crew would not land until 2027. On 7 December 2016 Mars One published an updated roadmap moving the first crewed mission to 2032, with the first robotic lander pushed to 2029. In roughly four years the first landing moved nine years further away, which is a faster rate of retreat than the calendar advances.

facts.label: What it actually bought
facts.value: Paper. What Mars One contracted for was concept studies: Paragon Space Development Corporation for life support concept studies, contracted 12 March 2013; Lockheed Martin for a demonstration lander concept study based on the NASA Phoenix design; and Surrey Satellite Technology Limited for a communications orbiter concept study. These were real contracts with real companies and they were studies. No metal was cut.

facts.label: No launch provider
facts.value: SpaceX was mentioned as a possible launch provider and there was contact in 2014, but SpaceX confirmed it had no contracts with Mars One and no Mars One launches on its manifest. A settlement plan with no signed launch agreement is a plan for a poster.

facts.label: The applicant numbers, as advertised
facts.value: Mars One said more than 200,000 people had applied, and that figure went round the world. Over 100,000 was being reported by August 2013 and the final claim settled at over 200,000. The number was central to the project's credibility: it was the evidence that the audience for the television show existed.

facts.label: The applicant numbers, as disputed
facts.value: Joseph Roche, an astrophysicist at Trinity College Dublin who reached the Mars 100 shortlist, said in March 2015 that the true number of completed applications was 2,761 rather than 200,000. English Wikipedia records that Mars One later confirmed the 2,761 figure in a YouTube video; the TechSpot report cited here does not say so. The two numbers are not the same measurement, and that is the point: one counts people who started something online, the other counts completed applications, and only the larger of the two was ever publicised.

facts.label: What else Roche said
facts.value: That what was supposed to be a regional interview process had been reduced to a ten minute Skype call, in which he was asked factual recall questions and given no psychological or psychometric testing; and that shortlisted candidates were asked to donate money they earned from media appearances back to Mars One. His stated reason for going public was that he did not want to be part of something that could damage the public perception of science.

facts.label: The selection rounds
facts.value: On 30 December 2013 Mars One named 1,058 candidates from 107 countries, 586 men and 472 women. In February 2015 that was cut to the Mars 100, fifty men and fifty women, after medical screening of 660. None of them were ever trained on flight hardware, because there was none.

facts.label: The television deal that collapsed
facts.value: Discussions with Endemol's Darlow Smithson Productions began in June 2014 for a reality series following the selection and training. The arrangement ended in February 2015, with a statement that the parties had been unable to reach agreement on the details. The funding model lost its only concrete commercial partner four years before the money ran out.

facts.label: The engineering verdict
facts.value: In October 2014 an MIT team presented an independent analysis. MIT News names Professor Olivier de Weck as its leader, working with the graduate students Sydney Do, Koki Ho, Andrew Owens and Samuel Schreiner; Do is the lead author of the paper. The analysis was presented at the International Astronautical Congress in Toronto. Their simulation had the first settler suffocating after an estimated 68 days, because the crops needed to feed the colony would drive oxygen levels dangerously high, the nitrogen needed to dilute the oxygen would be steadily consumed, and the habitat would eventually run out of gas to make up leaks. They also found that 15 Falcon Heavy launches would be needed for the initial supplies where Mars One assumed six.

facts.label: How MIT phrased it
facts.value: De Weck: "We're not saying, black and white, Mars One is infeasible," and "But we do think it's not really feasible under the assumptions they've made." Do, quoted in the same piece: "Our finding is the Mars One plan is inherently unsustainable and is hence infeasible." That distinction, between Mars being impossible and this plan being impossible, is the one most subsequent coverage lost.

facts.label: What Lansdorp conceded in public
facts.value: At a public debate against the MIT team in August 2015, reported by Dwayne Day in The Space Review, Lansdorp is described as admitting that the plan Mars One published was not really the plan it would use, acknowledging that he said different things to the press than at technical conferences, and conceding that he had no detailed technical plan.

facts.label: The bankruptcy
facts.value: Mars One Ventures AG, the Swiss for-profit arm which held the commercial rights, was declared bankrupt by a court in Basel on 15 January 2019. The collapse was not announced; it was noticed by a member of the public reading the register and reported in February. Trading in the shares, listed on the Frankfurt exchange, was suspended on 5 February 2019 for non-compliance with exchange rules over a 2017 share increase. That suspension date is not in the Engadget or BGR reporting cited here; it comes from English Wikipedia. Lansdorp said he was working with other parties to find a solution, and that the non-profit Mars One Foundation continued to exist but could not act without further investment.

timeline: Mars One becomes publicly visible. By early June international coverage is describing a Dutch venture that will land four people on Mars in 2023 and pay for it by selling the television rights. Bas Lansdorp is chief executive, Arno Wielders chief technical officer.

Paragon Space Development Corporation is contracted for life support concept studies. Lockheed Martin and Surrey Satellite Technology follow with lander and communications orbiter concept studies. All three are paper studies, and they are the closest Mars One ever comes to engineering.
Mars One names 1,058 candidates from 107 countries, 586 men and 472 women, selected from an applicant pool it describes as over 200,000.

Discussions begin with Endemol's Darlow Smithson Productions for a reality series following the selection and training of the settlers. This is the funding model becoming real for the first and only time.

Olivier de Weck, Sydney Do and colleagues present their independent feasibility analysis at the International Astronautical Congress in Toronto: first fatality by suffocation at an estimated 68 days, and 15 Falcon Heavy launches required against the six Mars One assumed.

Two things happen in the same month. Mars One announces the Mars 100 shortlist, fifty men and fifty women. And the Endemol arrangement ends, the parties unable to agree the details. The publicity peaks and the business model dies in the same four weeks.

Joseph Roche, a shortlisted candidate and an astrophysicist at Trinity College Dublin, goes public: 2,761 completed applications rather than 200,000, a ten minute Skype call in place of a regional interview, no psychological testing, and requests that candidates donate media earnings back to the organisation.
Lansdorp announces that the first crew will not land until 2027.

Mars One and the MIT team debate in public. Dwayne Day's account has Lansdorp conceding that the published plan is not the plan, that he says different things to journalists and to engineers, and that there is no detailed technical plan.
An updated roadmap moves the first crewed mission to 2032 and the first robotic lander to 2029. The first landing has now retreated nine years in four.
A court in Basel declares Mars One Ventures AG bankrupt. Nobody involved announces it.

Trading in Mars One Ventures shares is suspended in Frankfurt on 5 February, a date sourced to English Wikipedia rather than to the contemporaneous reporting. The bankruptcy is spotted by a member of the public reading the Swiss register and reported on 11 February. Lansdorp says he is working to find a solution; the Mars One Foundation survives on paper and does nothing further.

images.caption: A digital render of a white conical capsule carrying a small Mars One roundel, hanging above a rocky red plain on its descent engines with its landing legs out and a dust cloud rolling away downrange; on the Mars One roadmap page this illustrated the 2016 supply mission, which the accompanying text said would launch in January 2016 and land that October with 2,500 kilograms of spares, solar panels and supplies.
images.credit: Mars One Foundation; the concept art on the Mars One website is attributed to Bryan Versteeg of spacehabs.com, who English Wikipedia records created all the animations and illustrations used on it. Mars One published the images without a per-image credit line, so the attribution rests on that secondary record rather than on the file itself.

images.caption: A digital render of a low six-wheeled rover with a flat solar deck and a mast, driving across a rock-strewn red plain in low, raking light that throws long shadows; the Mars One roadmap text beside it described a 2018 settlement rover whose job was to find the exact site for the outpost and stream video to Earth continuously.
